scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Trasukha developed in the 19th century when Western European polkas were introduced to Belarus and merged with local East Slavic traditions.
It was popularized on the professional stage by Ihnat Bujnicki starting in 1907, who sought to preserve village traditions within the Belarusian National Theatre.
The dance is rooted in the 14th-century formation of Belarusian culture, drawing from ancient Russian and East Slavic rites.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: As a 'domestic' or 'actual' dance, Trasukha was originally performed in everyday life for social enjoyment.
It manifests the emotions and personality of the Belarusian people, often telling a story about life, work, or nature through its movements.
It is considered a 'playful' and 'dynamic' expression of the national soul.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Trasukha is a group dance performed by an unlimited number of participants, often in couples.
It is characterized by 'shaking' movements and the repetition of two or three dance figures.
The choreography is dynamic and cheerful, utilizing quick but easy movements.
Watch for Trasukha.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Ihnat Bujnicki is the central figure, having founded the first professional troupe in 1907 that included such folk dances.
Choreographer Larisa Aleksyutovich is noted for her classification of the dance, while other contributors to its staged development include K. Oleksyutovich and S. Grebenshchikov.
Trasukha is itself a regional Belarusian variant of the polka.
Trasukha is a subclass of East-Slavic folk dance and Belarusian dance.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Trasukha is parent of Polka: Trasukha is a Belarusian variant of the Czech polka.
Trasukha is sibling of Lyavonikha: Both are popular traditional Belarusian folk dances often performed together.
Trasukha is sibling of Kryzhachok: Another major Belarusian folk dance, though Kryzhachok is more ornamental/bird-mimicking.
